extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics / philosophy (Kantian aesthetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conceptual criteria for forming and evaluating aesthetic judgements about nature — especially distinguishing the Beautiful, the Sublime (mathematical and dynamical), the Pleasant, and the Absolutely Good — with attention to faculties (Imagination, Understanding, Reason), affective qualities, and necessary conditions for valid judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterested pleasure / subjective purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything which is to give disinterested pleasure to the merely reflective Judgement must bring with the representation of it, subjective and, as subjective, universally valid purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgement should be disinterested (not determined by practical or empirical interest) and must present a sense of purposiveness that is subjective yet claimed as universally valid. This is the formal condition tying aesthetic pleasure to a claim of common validity rather than private inclination. Anti-pattern: treating pleasurable response as grounded in personal desire or utility rather than a 'subjective purposiveness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure judgement must have no determining purpose of the object
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure judgement upon the sublime must have no purpose of the Object as its determining ground, if it is to be aesthetical and not mixed up with any judgement of Understanding or Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging something as sublime, one must avoid basing the judgement on the object's determinate purpose (practical, conceptual, or theoretical). If the judgement appeals to the object's function or aims, it becomes mixed with understanding/reason and ceases to be a pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monstrous vs Colossal (size relative to concept/purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: An object is 'monstrous' if by its size it destroys the purpose which constitutes the concept of it. The mere presentation of a concept is called 'colossal', which is almost too great for any presentation (bordering on the relatively monstrous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify very large objects by whether their magnitude undermines their conceptual purpose (monstrous) or merely strains presentation without destroying the concept (colossal). Example/anti-pattern: a mountain that makes the notion 'house' meaningless would be monstrous; a very large tree may be colossal but not monstrous. Use this distinction when evaluating whether size conflicts with the object's concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Sublime: imagination's inadequacy vs reason's demand for totality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mathematical Sublime arises when the Imagination's greatest effort to estimate magnitude is inadequate to present the object in a single intuition, while Reason requires totality and thinks the infinite as entirely given; thus the Imagination's inadequacy points to a supersensible Idea (absolute whole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify cases where magnitude (extension) strains the imagination so that it cannot grasp the manifold in a single intuition (e.g., earth's diameter, Milky Way). The feeling of the mathematical sublime is produced when imagination fails while reason posits an Idea of totality. Example: contemplating astronomical immensity triggers the mathematical sublime. Scoring note: emphasise whether the subject experiences the inadequacy (not merely numerical largeness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamical Sublime: nature as might that excites fear but leaves us safe
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature regarded as might that has no dominion over us is dynamically sublime. Nature can be judged dynamically sublime only insofar as it is represented as exciting fear (without real danger), thereby calling up a faculty in us that regards nature's might as not having dominion over our personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for impressions of overwhelming physical power (storms, volcanoes, tumultuous ocean, hurricanes) that raise the energies of the soul because the observer feels secure. The aesthetic pleasure comes from recognising an inner superiority (a moral or rational faculty) despite nature's might. Anti-pattern: real fear or immediate danger prevents an aesthetic judgement (it produces panic, not sublime appreciation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime feeling = respect: combined pain and pleasure; movement rather than restful contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of our incapacity to attain to an Idea (a law for us) is RESPECT. The feeling of the Sublime in nature is respect: a pain arising from the want of accordance between imagination and Reason, together with a pleasure arising from correspondence with rational Ideas; the mind feels moved (vibration) rather than at restful contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the affective quality: does the experience include painful awareness of inadequacy (imagination's limits) alongside a higher pleasure/esteem tied to reason's Ideas? Note the dynamic character (vibration, alternation of attraction and repulsion) distinguishing sublime responses from calm, restful appreciation of the Beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity resides in the subject's state of mind, not in the object
rubrics_metrics.description: True sublimity must be sought only in the mind of the [subject] judging, not in the natural Object, the judgement upon which occasions this state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a purportedly sublime object, focus on whether the subject's mental faculties (imagination, reason) are provoked into the particular relation (inadequacy + Idea) that yields the sublime, rather than assuming the property is inherent in the object. Anti-pattern: attributing sublimity solely to spectacular external features without considering the subject's cognitive-affective state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and moral prerequisites for judging the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement upon the sublime in nature needs culture (more than the judgement upon the Beautiful) and postulates a susceptibility of the mind for Ideas; without development of moral Ideas what the cultivated call sublime will present to the uneducated merely as terrible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the subject's cultural development and moral feeling: a cultivated sensibility able to relate imagination to Reason is required to experience the sublime. Example: an uneducated peasant may only perceive danger/terror where the cultured perceive sublime elevation. Scoring: account for evaluator/viewer's level of moral/intellectual cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgments claim a priori universal validity (modality of necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the modality of aesthetic judgements (necessity claimed for them) lies an important moment: we can ascribe necessity to aesthetic judgements and recognise in them an a priori principle, raising them out of empirical psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming or assessing aesthetic judgements, note whether the judgement implicitly claims universal assent (not merely subjective preference). This claim is grounded in a priori principles of the faculty of judgement rather than empirical contingencies. Anti-pattern: treating aesthetic claims as purely empirical or relative without any claim to universal validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of feeling-types: Pleasant, Beautiful, Sublime, Absolutely Good
rubrics_metrics.description: In reference to the feeling of pleasure an object is to be classified as either pleasant, or beautiful, or sublime, or good (absolutely). The pleasant is a motive of desire and depends on quantity; the beautiful requires representation of a certain quality (purposiveness) and cultivates attention to purposiveness; the sublime consists in the relation by which the sensible is judged available for a possible supersensible use; the absolutely good is judged by moral feeling and has a modal necessity a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to categorize responses: Pleasant = sensory/quantitative; Beautiful = formal purposiveness and disinterested pleasure; Sublime = relation to supersensible Ideas (mathematical or dynamical); Absolutely Good = moral, determinate, a priori necessity. Apply the correct category when evaluating works or experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different faculty relations: Beautiful = Imagination→Understanding; Sublime = Imagination→Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetical Judgement in judging the Beautiful refers the Imagination in its free play to the Understanding, to harmonise with concepts; when judging the Sublime the same faculty refers itself to the Reason so that it may be subjectively in accordance with its Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which cognitive faculty is being engaged: Beautiful judgments emphasize harmony between imagination and understanding (formal purposiveness), while Sublime judgments emphasize the relation and conflict between imagination and Reason (Ideas, the supersensible). This helps diagnose whether an aesthetic reaction is properly 'beautiful' or 'sublime.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety / absence of real danger as a condition for experiencing the Dynamical Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: If nature is to be judged by us as dynamically sublime, it must be represented as exciting fear (although it is not true conversely that every object which excites fear is regarded in our aesthetical judgement as sublime). The sight of fearful natural powers is more attractive provided only that we are in security; he who fears can form no judgement about the Sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the subject is not actually endangered; only contemplated danger (fear imagined while objectively safe) can yield the pleasurable, elevating effect of the dynamical sublime. Actual fear that drives flight or panic disqualifies the aesthetic appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime as moral-cognitive cultivation: prepares esteem opposed to sensible interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime prepares us to esteem something highly even in opposition to our own (sensible) interest, while the Beautiful prepares us to love disinterestedly something, even nature itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the ethical or educative effects of aesthetic experience, note that the sublime tends to foster esteem and a sense of moral or rational elevation (opposed to immediate sensible interest), whereas the beautiful fosters disinterested love and cultivation. Use this to judge the moral or formative value attributed to an artwork or natural spectacle.
